title: South African care work converts gender, household infrastructure and dependency into unequal time and labour-market room
source_unit: Statistics South Africa, Gender Series Volume XIII: Gender Disparities in Care Work in South Africa, 2026, with official summary and publication metadata
geography: South Africa; national gender, household, labour-market, education and infrastructure indicators

denominator.unit: South African population and dependency-ratio frame reported by Statistics South Africa

female_population_share_2026.unit: percent of population female in 2026, versus 49.1% male

old_age_dependency_change.unit: older persons per 100 working-age persons, as reported

observations.method: Statistics South Africa thematic report and official summary using available official demographic and household statistics; the publication uses proxy indicators in the absence of recent time-use data.
observations.uncertainty: Dependency ratios describe population structure, not who provides care, how many hours are supplied, or the quality and intensity of care.
observations.subgroup: South African population, households and age groups; non-urban dependency ratios are reported as higher than urban ratios.
observations.counterinterpretation: A rising working-age share may expand potential care capacity, while ageing and household composition may still increase unpaid-care demands; population structure alone cannot determine household burden.

denominator.unit: South African households by sex of household head in the official summary

female_headed_households.unit: share of households headed by females

female_headed_no_employed_member.unit: share of female-headed households with no employed member

male_headed_no_employed_member.unit: share of male-headed households with no employed member

care_income_mechanism.value: care responsibilities and household employment structure jointly shape the money available to absorb care

observations.method: Statistics South Africa gender-series comparison of household structure and employment status using official household indicators.
observations.uncertainty: Household head status is not a direct measure of caregiving, household decision power, income amount, or within-household resource distribution.
observations.subgroup: Female-headed and male-headed South African households.
observations.counterinterpretation: The association between household headship and employment does not identify whether care caused non-employment or whether employment status shaped household structure.

observations.period: 2025; education interruption and gendered family commitments

denominator.unit: South African children aged 7-18 not attending an educational institution in the official summary

female_family_commitment_reason.unit: percent of females aged 7-18 not attending school citing family commitments as the main reason

male_family_commitment_reason.unit: percent of males aged 7-18 not attending school citing family commitments as the main reason

education_care_conversion.value: family commitments appear as a gendered reason for non-attendance while males more often cite poor academic performance

observations.method: Official Statistics South Africa summary of Gender Series XIII education non-attendance indicators.
observations.uncertainty: The summary does not provide the full denominator, sample design, confidence intervals, duration of non-attendance, or whether family commitments involve care, domestic work, income work or other obligations.
observations.subgroup: South African females and males aged 7-18 who were not attending an educational institution.
observations.counterinterpretation: The gender difference is descriptive and does not prove that care responsibilities caused educational exit or later labour-market disadvantage.

observations.period: 2015-2026; paid care, earnings and infrastructure effort

denominator.unit: South African labour-market, household-expenditure and water-access indicators in the official summary

female_paid_care_concentration.value: women dominated domestic work, nursing, teaching and social work in both 2015 and 2026

earnings_change.value: median monthly earnings rose by R1,500 for males and R1,400 for females between 2018 and 2024

preprimary_expenditure_change.value: average pre-primary education expenditure rose from R7,785 in 2015 to R8,069 in 2023

female_headed_stream_water.unit: households fetching water from a stream or river

under_30_minutes_water.value: 79.6% of male-headed households versus 69.8% of female-headed households
under_30_minutes_water.unit: households spending less than 30 minutes fetching water

observations.method: Statistics South Africa thematic synthesis of labour, earnings, household expenditure, water access and household infrastructure indicators; it is not a single respondent-level time-use dataset.
observations.uncertainty: Occupational concentration, expenditure and water-collection indicators do not measure unpaid-care hours, causality, care quality, total household budgets or the effectiveness of infrastructure improvements.
observations.subgroup: South African workers and households, disaggregated by sex of household head and selected sectors/geographies.
observations.counterinterpretation: Female concentration in paid-care occupations can reflect both labour-market opportunity and occupational segregation; lower water-collection time may indicate improved access without proving reduced total care work.

related_sources.claim: Official Statistics South Africa publication page for the full Gender Series XIII report, published 6 August 2026.
Official publication description stating that the report uses available official statistics and proxy indicators because recent time-use data are unavailable.

boundary: This record adds a gendered care-conversion mechanism: demographic dependency, household employment, family commitments, paid-care concentration and infrastructure effort shape who has usable time and labour-market room. Statistics South Africa states that recent time-use data are unavailable and the report uses proxy indicators; this record therefore does not estimate unpaid-care hours, causal effects, within-household bargaining, care quality or a complete care economy.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: The official Statistics South Africa care-work article, publication page and publication metadata were reviewed for demographic dependency, household employment, education non-attendance, paid-care concentration, earnings, expenditure, water access and time-use limitations.
